title: What Do We Miss When We Study Plants Without Studying People?
excerpt: Justin Nolan and Nancy Turner’s chapter on Ethnobotany: The Study of People-Plant Relationships made me reflect on how environmental knowledge can become fragmented when we separate the ecological from the cultural.
content:
RAZAQ-RICH-TEXT/1
{"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"What Do We Miss When We Study Plants Without Studying People?","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Justin Nolan and Nancy Turner’s chapter on Ethnobotany: "},{"type":"text","text":"The Study of People-Plant Relationships","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":" made me reflect on how environmental knowledge can become fragmented when we separate the ecological from the cultural."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"People often study plants by species, distribution, chemical composition, productivity, medicinal properties, and conservation status. While these forms of knowledge are important, Nolan and Turner remind us that plants also exist within human relationships: as food, medicine, memory, identity, ceremony, livelihood, language, and cultural continuity."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This is what makes ethnobotany interesting. It does not treat plants as isolated biological objects. Instead, it asks how people know, use, name, value, remember, and sustain relationships with plants over time. The field itself is interdisciplinary, connecting ecology, conservation biology, anthropology, environmental studies, geography, linguistics, and other disciplines."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"I found the authors’ emphasis on participation and collaboration especially important."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Many ethnobotanical studies can't be conducted solely in labs, archives, or offices. Researchers often engage directly with communities, immersing themselves in the environments where they practice knowledge daily. Nolan and Turner define participant observation as activities such as gardening, gathering, fishing, preparing meals, collecting water, and sharing everyday routines with community members. This hands-on involvement allows researchers to observe knowledge deeply rooted in daily life, so much so that community members may never consider explaining these insights in a standard interview."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"That idea is worth pausing over."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Not all-important knowledge announces itself as knowledge","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":"."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Sometimes it is carried in practice."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"It may be present in how a plant is harvested, when it is gathered, who gathers it, what is left untouched, how it is prepared, what stories accompany it, and the responsibilities that govern its use."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Therefore, if researchers enter such settings with only predetermined questions, some of the most meaningful knowledge may remain invisible, not because it is absent, but because the research process was not designed to recognize it."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Nolan and Turner also explain why this matters for sustainability. They note that cultural philosophies and worldviews can shape collective behaviour toward other species and the environment, and that Indigenous and local knowledge systems have become increasingly important for biodiversity conservation and sustainability."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This suggests that conserving biodiversity may require more than protecting individual species or ecosystems. It may also require safeguarding the relationships, practices, languages, memories, and knowledge systems through which communities have learned to live with those species."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The authors also raise an ethical issue that should not be overlooked. As ethnobotany developed, greater attention has been paid to community priorities, ethical protocols, equitable partnerships, and the responsible sharing of benefits derived from traditional ecological knowledge."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"That shifts the role of the researcher."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The researcher is not simply someone who arrives, records knowledge, and leaves with information. Meaningful research requires relationships, responsibility, permission, reciprocity, and respect for the people whose knowledge makes the research possible."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Perhaps this is one of the most important insights I take from ethnobotany:"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"“To understand an ecosystem, it may not be enough to know what grows there. We may also need to understand the relationships that have allowed people and plants to live together over generations”."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"A plant can be a biological species."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"But it can also be medicine."},{"type":"hardBreak"},{"type":"text","text":"Memory."},{"type":"hardBreak"},{"type":"text","text":"Food."},{"type":"hardBreak"},{"type":"text","text":"Identity."},{"type":"hardBreak"},{"type":"text","text":"Responsibility."},{"type":"hardBreak"},{"type":"text","text":"And relationship."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Sustainability becomes richer when we learn to see all of these dimensions together."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Reflection on Justin M. Nolan and Nancy J. Turner’s “Ethnobotany: The Study of People-Plant Relationships.”","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#Ethnobotany                                               #IndigenousKnowledge","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#Sustainability                                            #TraditionalEcologicalKnowledge","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#Biodiversity                                                #PeoplePlantRelationships","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#EnvironmentalKnowledge","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]}]}

title: What If the Land Is Also a Teacher?
excerpt: We often confine serious learning to university classrooms, books, formal instruction, and recognized experts. The author of Land as Pedagogy invites us to consider a very different understanding. Writing from a Nishnaabeg context, Simpson shows that learning can also emerge from the land, relationships, observation, experience, community, language, spirituality, and practice.
content:
RAZAQ-RICH-TEXT/1
{"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"What If the Land Is Also a Teacher?","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Leanne Betasamosake Simpson’s article, “Land as Pedagogy,” made me reflect on a question we rarely ask in conventional education: "},{"type":"text","text":"Where does knowledge come from?","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"We often confine serious learning to university classrooms, books, formal instruction, and recognized experts. The author of Land as Pedagogy invites us to consider a very different understanding. Writing from a Nishnaabeg context, Simpson shows that learning can also emerge from the land, relationships, observation, experience, community, language, spirituality, and practice."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Her story of Kwezens brings this understanding vividly to life."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Kwezens’s learning process does not begin with a textbook, a lecture, or a formal lesson. She learns through curiosity, attention, experimentation, and relationships. She learns with and from maple trees and from the community around her, where knowledge is modeled in everyday interactions with creation. Simpson describes this as more than “land-based education.” Her argument goes deeper: "},{"type":"text","text":"the land must become the pedagogy.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"That distinction matters."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"If we treat land only as the place where learning occurs, it remains little more than a backdrop. Simpson invites us to understand something deeper: land is not simply a setting for learning but part of the relationship that makes learning possible. From this perspective, knowledge is not produced only within institutions and then applied to the world. It can also emerge through living, observing, participating, listening, practicing, and sustaining relationships with the land and the beings who share it."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Simpson’s discussion of aki deepens this idea. Within the Nishnaabeg worldview she describes, aki is profoundly relational, encompassing landforms, plants, animals, spirits, sounds, thoughts, feelings, energies, ecologies, and the networks that connect them. Knowledge, therefore, cannot be easily separated from the relationships through which it is generated."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This raises an important question for sustainability."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Much environmental thinking understandably relies on observation, measurement, management, and intervention. Simpson invites us to consider another possibility: what might change if we understood ourselves not only as observers of environmental relationships, but as participants within the relationships we are trying to sustain?"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Her discussion of Nanabush makes this insight even more practical. In this account, learning requires engagement. One learns by going out, observing, experimenting, visiting, building relationships, and becoming invested in the world one seeks to understand. Simpson presents this not merely as a method of acquiring information but as part of learning to live responsibly within a specific relational context."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Perhaps this is one of the deeper lessons sustainability can take from Indigenous knowledge traditions:"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"We may not learn how to care for the Earth only by studying it from a distance."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Some knowledge may require presence.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Some understanding may require relationship.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"And some responsibilities may only become visible when we learn to pay attention differently.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Simpson’s work therefore leaves us with a question that goes beyond education:"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"If the land can teach, are we still capable of listening?","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#IndigenousKnowledge                               #LandAsPedagogy "}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#Sustainability                                               #IndigenousWaysOfKnowing "}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#EnvironmentalLearning                            #Relationality "}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#LeanneSimpson"}]}]}

title: Perhaps Sustainability Needs a Different Story
excerpt:
We often talk about the environmental problems as though their central challenge were developing better technologies, strengthening government and international policies, improving institutional quality, or finding alternative ways to manage natural resources.
This article by Thomas King made me wonder whether the problem lies somewhere deeper: in the stories through which we have learned to understand ourselves and our place in the world.

{"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Perhaps Sustainability Needs a Different Story","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"We often talk about the environmental problems as though their central challenge were developing better technologies, strengthening government and international policies, improving institutional quality, or finding alternative ways to manage natural resources."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This article by Thomas King made me wonder whether the problem lies somewhere deeper: in the stories through which we have learned to understand ourselves and our place in the world."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"In “You’ll Never Believe What Happened” Is Always a Great Way to Start, the author does not simply use stories as illustrations. He demonstrates what stories can do. In King’s explanation, stories carry assumptions about who we are, what matters, how beings should relate to one another, and what kind of world we believe is possible."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"King’s comparison of creation stories is particularly striking. He contrasts the Genesis creation story, which he presents as hierarchical and characterized by separation, with the story of Charm, in which creation unfolds through relationship, cooperation, participation, and balance. His comparison raises an important question: "},{"type":"text","text":"might a world imagined through competition produce different relationships than one imagined through cooperation?","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"That question deserves attention in sustainability."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Perhaps some of our environmental challenges are not simply failures of technology, policy, or institutions. They may also reflect deeper cultural narratives that position Earth primarily as a resource, subordinate other beings to human purposes, and associate progress with increasing possession, consumption, and control."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"If so, sustainability requires more than repairing environmental damage after it occurs. It may also require reconsidering the stories that make certain relationships with the Earth seem natural, inevitable, or acceptable."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This is where I find Indigenous knowledge traditions especially important. In their distinct cultural contexts, they should not be treated merely as additional information to insert into existing sustainability frameworks, because they invite a more fundamental act of listening to Land, relationships, responsibilities, other beings, community, and ways of understanding human existence that do not necessarily begin with human dominance."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"King does not propose another technical formula for sustainability. His intervention is more demanding: "},{"type":"text","text":"he asks us to examine the stories from which our solutions emerge.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Hence, before asking only, "},{"type":"text","text":"What new solution can we introduce?","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":" perhaps we should also ask:"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"What story has brought us here","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":"?"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"What relationships has that story taught us to normalize","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":"?"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"And perhaps most importantly:"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Are there other stories we have not listened to carefully enough","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":"?"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Sometimes a sustainable future may begin not by speaking louder, but by learning to listen differently."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Reflection on Thomas King’s “You’ll Never Believe What title: Whose Knowledge, Whose Terms?
excerpt: Growing recognition shows that Indigenous knowledge has an important place in environmental management, sustainability, research, and decision-making.
content:
RAZAQ-RICH-TEXT/1
{"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Whose Knowledge, Whose Terms?","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"When recognition does not necessarily mean respect","marks":[{"type":"bold"},{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Growing recognition shows that Indigenous knowledge has an important place in environmental management, sustainability, research, and decision-making."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"At first glance, this seems like progress."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"But Leanne Simpson’s article "},{"type":"text","text":"“Aboriginal Peoples and Knowledge: Decolonizing Our Processes”","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":" raises a more uncomfortable question: what happens when institutions welcome Indigenous knowledge, but Indigenous peoples lack equivalent authority over how that knowledge is defined, interpreted, and used?"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Simpson’s concern is not simply whether institutions include Indigenous knowledge. Her Question focuses more on the conditions under which inclusion occurs."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Writing from an Anishinaabe perspective, she reflects on the growing interest in Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) across universities, environmental impact assessments, natural resource management, government agencies, and development projects. She notes that this recognition follows a long history of ignoring, undermining, and dismissing Indigenous knowledge. Yet she also warns that recognition can create another problem when outsiders focus primarily on parts of Indigenous knowledge that can be extracted and fitted into existing scientific or institutional frameworks."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This distinction is important."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"When knowledge is separated from the relationships, values, ethics, spirituality, culture, and processes that give it meaning, something fundamental can be lost. Simpson describes this process as the “scientizing” of Indigenous knowledge-reducing a broader knowledge system to information or data that can be more easily incorporated into another framework."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"That idea deserves serious reflection."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Knowledge is not always something that can simply be collected, transferred, and inserted elsewhere without changing what it means.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"A story separated from the relationships that give it meaning may become merely text."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Knowledge of a plant removed from the community, language, practices, responsibilities, and worldview surrounding it may become mere data. Likewise, Indigenous knowledge separated from the people who hold, interpret, and live that knowledge may become something very different from what was originally shared."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Simpson pushes this argument further by drawing attention to authority. She describes situations in which Elders and community members contribute knowledge to research or environmental assessments, yet scientists, consultants, or external institutions ultimately determine how that knowledge is interpreted and whether it will influence decisions. In such circumstances, participation exists, but control remains elsewhere."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This raises an important distinction for sustainability:"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Being invited into the conversation is not necessarily the same as having a meaningful voice in the decision. ","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":"And having one's knowledge recorded is not necessarily the same as having that knowledge respected."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Simpson therefore invites us to move beyond the language of simply “including Indigenous knowledge.” The more demanding questions are:"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Who defines what counts as useful knowledge?","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Who decides what can be shared?","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Who interprets what has been shared?","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Who determines how that knowledge will be used?","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"And who ultimately holds the authority to make decisions?","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Her alternative is not merely to improve the extraction of Indigenous knowledge. She argues for recognizing Indigenous peoples' own paradigms, philosophies, ways of knowing, methodologies, cultural protocols, and decision-making processes. Rather than inserting fragments of Indigenous knowledge into frameworks developed elsewhere, she points toward processes grounded in the communities from which that knowledge originates."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Simpson’s description of her own role as a researcher is powerful. In working with Elders and knowledge holders, she does not automatically position herself as the expert. She describes herself as a student and emphasizes listening, patience, cultural protocol, and the authority of Elders and community experts."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"That challenges a deeply familiar idea of expertise."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Perhaps responsible research is not always demonstrated by how much we can extract, explain, document, or interpret."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Sometimes responsibility may begin with recognizing "},{"type":"text","text":"when we are not the authority.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"For sustainability, this lesson is significant."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"If we genuinely believe that diverse knowledge traditions can help address environmental challenges, recognition cannot stop at citation, consultation, or the collection of knowledge."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"It must also involve questions of "},{"type":"text","text":"relationship, consent, context, responsibility, ","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]},{"type":"text","text":"and"},{"type":"text","text":" authority.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Perhaps the deeper lesson from Simpson’s article is this:"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The question is not simply whether Indigenous knowledge has been included. The question is whether the people to whom that knowledge belongs still have the power to determine what it means and what happens to it.","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Recognition matters."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"But recognition without authority can still leave the underlying relationship unchanged."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":"justify"},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Reflection on Leanne Simpson’s “Aboriginal Peoples and Knowledge: Decolonizing Our Processes.”","marks":[{"type":"italic"}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#IndigenousKnowledge                              #Decolonization"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#TraditionalEcologicalKnowledge            #Sustainability #IndigenousWaysOfKnowing                   #ResearchEthics"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"#SelfDetermination                                      #EnvironmentalGovernance"}]}]}
